LONDON, England (CNN) -- What recession? Christie's, the famed auction house, this week sold a nearly 36-carat diamond for $24.3 million, which it said was the highest price for a diamond sold at auction. The 35.56-carat diamond dates back to the 17th century. The previous record was a mere $16.5 million for a 100-carat diamond in 1995, Christie's said. "In the midst of these challenging times, we were thrilled to achieve an historic price for an historic diamond," said Francois Curiel, chairman of Christie's Europe and auctioneer for Wednesday's sale. The 35.56-carat Wittelsbach blue diamond, dating to the 17th century, was purchased by international jeweler Laurence Graff, the auction house said in a release. Graff was bidding against Aleks Paul of Essex Global Trading, a professional of Russian origin based in New York, Christie's said. "Known as 'Der Blaue Wittelsbacher' since 1722, it is one of very few diamonds which can claim 17th century heritage, incredible rarity and exceptional beauty." The diamond, mined in India nearly 400 years ago, has been privately owned since 1964. Until 1723, Christie's said, all diamonds worn by European royalty came from India. The diamond has a royal lineage. Christie's traces it thus: King Philip IV of Spain (1605-1665) selected the diamond in 1664 as part of a dowry for his daughter, the Infanta Margarita Teresa (1651-1673). She had become engaged to Leopold I of Austria (1640-1705), who later became Holy Roman Emperor. When she died in 1673, her husband retained the diamond, which was passed on to his heirs. In 1722, the diamond entered the Wittelsbach family when the Archduchess Maria Amalia of Austria (1701-1756) married the Bavarian Crown Prince, Charles Albert (1697-1745). It was worn by successive rulers until the abdication of King Ludwig III (1845-1921) in 1918. The world's largest deep blue diamond is the "Hope Diamond," a 45.52-carat stone housed at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, DC. Diamonds apparently are recession-proof. Christie's reported jewelry sales of $226 million for the first half of 2008, calling it "the best jewelry season ever seen at auction." Sales for the first six months of this year marked a 32 percent increase over the same period in 2007, Christie's said. According to Christie's, key diamonds the company sold in the first half of 2008 included a 13.39-carat fancy intense blue diamond that fetched $8.9 million in Geneva on May 14 and the pear-shaped potentially flawless 38-carat Onassis diamond, which sold for $7.1 million on June 11 in London.

LONDON, England (CNN) — Recession or not, buyers at Christie’s showed no hesitation this week: the renowned auction house sold an almost 36-carat diamond for $24.3 million, a figure it described as the highest auction price ever paid for a diamond.

The gem, a 35.56-carat stone with origins in the 17th century, surpassed the earlier auction record of $16.5 million, set in 1995 for a 100-carat diamond, according to Christie’s.

“During these difficult times, we are delighted to have reached a historic price for a historic diamond,” said Francois Curiel, chairman of Christie’s Europe and the auctioneer who handled Wednesday’s sale.

Christie’s said in a statement that the 35.56-carat Wittelsbach blue diamond, which dates from the 1600s, was bought by international jeweler Laurence Graff. His rival bidder was Aleks Paul of Essex Global Trading, a New York-based professional of Russian origin, the auction house said.

The stone has been known since 1722 as “Der Blaue Wittelsbacher.” Christie’s described it as one of the rare diamonds able to combine documented 17th-century history, extreme scarcity and extraordinary beauty.

Mined in India nearly four centuries ago, the diamond has remained in private hands since 1964. Christie’s noted that, until 1723, every diamond worn by European royalty had come from India.

The diamond’s history is tied to European royal families. According to Christie’s account, King Philip IV of Spain, who lived from 1605 to 1665, chose the stone in 1664 as part of the dowry for his daughter, the Infanta Margarita Teresa, who lived from 1651 to 1673. She was engaged to Leopold I of Austria, born in 1640 and deceased in 1705, who later became Holy Roman Emperor.

After Margarita Teresa died in 1673, Leopold kept the diamond, and it was later inherited by his descendants. In 1722, the jewel became part of the Wittelsbach family through the marriage of Archduchess Maria Amalia of Austria, who lived from 1701 to 1756, to Bavarian Crown Prince Charles Albert, who lived from 1697 to 1745.

The diamond continued to be worn by a succession of rulers until 1918, when King Ludwig III, who lived from 1845 to 1921, abdicated.

The largest deep-blue diamond in the world is the Hope Diamond, a 45.52-carat gem kept at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C.

Diamonds, it seems, may be resistant to economic downturns. Christie’s said its jewelry sales reached $226 million in the first half of 2008, describing the period as “the best jewelry season ever seen at auction.” The company said sales during the first six months of 2008 were 32 percent higher than in the same period of 2007.

Among the major diamonds Christie’s sold in early 2008 were a 13.39-carat fancy intense blue diamond, which brought $8.9 million in Geneva on May 14, and the pear-shaped, potentially flawless 38-carat Onassis diamond, which sold in London on June 11 for $7.1 million.

The 35.56-carat Wittelsbach blue diamond sold Wednesday at Christie’s in London for **$24.3 million**, setting a new auction record for any diamond, the auction house said.

The buyer was London jeweler **Laurence Graff**, who outbid competitors for the historic gem after intense bidding. The sale surpassed the previous diamond auction record and underscored the resilience of the market for exceptional jewels, even as recession fears grip much of the world.

The Wittelsbach diamond, a deep grayish-blue stone, is prized not only for its size and color but also for its royal history. The gem is believed to have originated in India and was once part of the Austrian and Bavarian crown jewels. It passed through the hands of European royalty for centuries before disappearing from public view for decades.

Christie’s had described the diamond as one of the most important historic gems ever offered at auction. Blue diamonds are among the rarest colored diamonds, and stones of this size and provenance almost never come to market.

The record-setting price comes at a time when luxury markets have shown signs of strain, with collectors and investors becoming more cautious amid the global credit crunch. But auction specialists say the most exceptional objects can still command extraordinary sums.

“This result demonstrates that true rarity continues to attract buyers,” Christie’s said after the sale.

The Wittelsbach’s final price — including commission — reached **$24.3 million**, making it one of the most valuable gemstones ever sold publicly and a striking reminder that, even in a recession, some treasures remain in high demand.

**Historic Wittelsbach Blue Diamond Sells for Record Price at Auction**

**London —** The legendary **Wittelsbach blue diamond**, one of the most storied gems in European royal history, sold at auction for **£16.4 million**, or about **$24.3 million**, setting a world auction record for a diamond at the time of its sale.

The 35.56-carat, cushion-shaped, deep blue diamond was purchased in 2008 at **Christie’s in London** by British billionaire jeweler **Laurence Graff**, founder of Graff Diamonds. After acquiring it, Graff renamed the gem the **Wittelsbach-Graff Diamond**.

### A Royal Jewel With Centuries of History

The Wittelsbach diamond’s history reaches back to the great royal courts of Europe. Believed to have originated from the famed **Golconda mines of India**, the same source associated with several of the world’s most celebrated diamonds, the stone first appeared in European royal records in the 17th century.

It is widely believed to have entered the Habsburg dynasty through **Infanta Margarita Teresa of Spain**, who married **Leopold I, Holy Roman Emperor**, in 1666. The diamond later passed into the possession of the **Wittelsbach family**, rulers of Bavaria, through marriage ties between the Austrian and Bavarian royal houses.

For generations, the stone was part of the **Bavarian Crown Jewels**. It was mounted in royal ornaments and eventually placed in the **Bavarian royal crown**, becoming a symbol of dynastic prestige. After the fall of the Bavarian monarchy following World War I, the diamond remained associated with the former royal house before eventually disappearing from public view for decades.

Its reappearance at auction drew intense interest from collectors, historians, and gem experts because of both its rarity and its provenance.

### Price and Buyer

At Christie’s, the Wittelsbach blue diamond sold for:

- **£16.4 million**
- Approximately **$24.3 million**
- Buyer: **Laurence Graff**

The sale surpassed previous auction records for diamonds at the time, reflecting not only the gem’s size and color but also its extraordinary royal history.

### Recutting and Controversy

After the purchase, Laurence Graff had the diamond recut to improve its clarity, symmetry, and brilliance. The stone was reduced from **35.56 carats** to **31.06 carats** and was graded by the Gemological Institute of America as **Fancy Deep Blue** and **internally flawless**.

The recutting was controversial. Some historians and gem experts argued that altering such a historically important royal jewel diminished its authenticity as an artifact. Others defended the decision, saying it enhanced the diamond’s optical beauty and market value.

### Comparison With Other Famous Diamonds

The Wittelsbach-Graff Diamond is often compared with the world’s most famous blue diamond, the **Hope Diamond**.

- **Hope Diamond**: 45.52 carats, Fancy Deep grayish blue, housed at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C. It is larger than the Wittelsbach-Graff and arguably more famous, but it has not been sold publicly in modern times.
- **Wittelsbach-Graff Diamond**: 31.06 carats after recutting, Fancy Deep Blue, privately owned after its auction purchase by Laurence Graff.

Both stones are believed to have originated in India and have been linked to European royalty. Their similar color and historic backgrounds have long led to speculation about whether they may have come from the same original rough diamond, though this has never been definitively proven.

The Wittelsbach-Graff also stands alongside other celebrated colored diamonds, including:

- **The Pink Star**: A 59.60-carat pink diamond that sold for $71.2 million in 2017, setting a record for any diamond or gemstone sold at auction.
- **The Oppenheimer Blue**: A 14.62-carat Fancy Vivid Blue diamond that sold for about $57.5 million in 2016.
- **The Blue Moon of Josephine**: A 12.03-carat Fancy Vivid Blue diamond that sold for about $48.5 million in 2015.
- **The Dresden Green Diamond**: A 41-carat natural green diamond housed in Dresden, Germany, famous for its rare color and royal provenance.

### A Gem of Beauty and Power

The sale of the Wittelsbach blue diamond marked one of the most dramatic moments in the modern colored-diamond market. More than a gemstone, it is a relic of European dynastic power, linking the courts of Spain, Austria, and Bavaria with the modern world of elite collectors.

Its record-setting auction price reflected a rare combination of qualities: exceptional color, large size, historic provenance, and royal mystique. Even amid a market filled with spectacular diamonds, the Wittelsbach-Graff remains one of the most important blue diamonds ever known.

**Luxury News | Diamonds Defy the Downturn as Christie’s 2008 Sales Shine**

*London/New York —* At a time when global markets were reeling, banks were collapsing and luxury retailers were bracing for a long chill, one corner of the high-end market delivered a strikingly different message: exceptional diamonds remained in demand.

Christie’s 2008 jewelry sales offered a vivid example of how the rarest stones can behave less like discretionary purchases and more like portable, global stores of wealth. Despite the financial crisis, the auction house’s jewelry department recorded hundreds of millions of dollars in sales that year, led by fierce bidding for museum-quality gems and signed jewels.

The defining moment came in December 2008, when the **Wittelsbach Diamond**, a legendary **35.56-carat deep grayish-blue diamond**, sold at Christie’s London for **£16.4 million**, or about **$24.3 million** at the time. The result set a then-world record auction price for any diamond and became one of the most powerful symbols of resilience in the luxury market during the recession.

The buyer was later identified as London jeweler **Laurence Graff**, one of the world’s best-known diamond dealers. His acquisition of the Wittelsbach underscored a key truth of the ultra-luxury market: in periods of turmoil, collectors and investors often retreat from mass luxury but continue to compete aggressively for assets that are genuinely rare, historically important and difficult to replicate.

The Wittelsbach was no ordinary jewel. With a royal European provenance dating back centuries, the blue diamond had passed through the collections of Spanish and Bavarian royalty. Its combination of size, color, history and mystique placed it in the highest tier of collectible gems — the sort of asset that can attract buyers even when broader consumer confidence is weak.

Christie’s jewelry results in 2008 reinforced that point. While mainstream luxury spending softened, the auction market for top-quality stones continued to benefit from international wealth, particularly from buyers seeking tangible assets amid currency volatility and collapsing equity markets. Large colored diamonds, rare white diamonds, natural pearls and signed period jewels by houses such as Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels remained highly sought after.

Auction specialists often note that the diamond market is not uniformly recession-proof. Commercial-quality stones and ordinary jewelry can suffer when consumers pull back. But the very top end — blue diamonds, pink diamonds, flawless large white stones and jewels with royal or historic provenance — operates by different rules. Supply is extremely limited, ownership is global, and wealthy collectors may view such pieces as both status symbols and long-term stores of value.

The 2008 sale of the Wittelsbach Diamond captured that dynamic perfectly. In one of the darkest months of the financial crisis, bidders were still willing to pay a record price for a stone that could not simply be replaced by another luxury product.

For the high-jewelry market, the lesson was clear: recessions can punish fashion-driven luxury, but rarity remains powerful. When a diamond is important enough, the world’s wealthiest buyers do not disappear — they compete.
